# rpspanel

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/adebayomoses/rpspanel/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/adebayomoses/rpspanel/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![r-universe](https://adebayomoses.r-universe.dev/badges/rpspanel)](https://adebayomoses.r-universe.dev/rpspanel)
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23480612.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23480612)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/rpspanel)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rpspanel)
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/rpspanel)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rpspanel)
[![Project Status: Active - The project has reached a stable, usable state and is being actively developed.](https://www.repostatus.org/badges/latest/active.svg)](https://www.repostatus.org/#active)
<!-- badges: end -->

**rpspanel** gives researchers a documented, reproducible US state-by-year
energy-economy panel (50 states + DC), with Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS)
stringency measures, in a few lines of R.

* **One call, one panel.** `build_panel()` merges EIA energy use, prices and
  production (SEDS), electricity generation and retail sales, state CO2
  emissions, and BEA GDP, income and population.
* **Reproducible.** Every variable's source, vintage and transformation is
  recorded; `codebook()` and `cite_sources()` document the panel. Downloads
  are cached so vintages stay pinned.
* **Better policy measures.** `rps_stringency()` returns adoption, nominal,
  coverage-adjusted and incremental (Yin and Powers 2010) requirements, plus
  design-flexibility indicators.
* **Fits existing tools.** `as_pdata()` hands the panel to `plm`, `fixest`
  or `csdm`; `export_panel()` writes CSV, Stata or Parquet.

Documentation: <https://adebayomoses.github.io/rpspanel/>

## Why rpspanel?

Studies of how US state energy policy affects growth and emissions usually
rebuild the same state-by-year dataset by hand. Energy use and prices come from
the EIA, GDP and population from the BEA, emissions from the EIA's state CO2
data and renewable policy rules from DSIRE or Berkeley Lab. Each source has its
own format, units, state codes and release schedule, and the cleaning code is
rarely published. Renewable Portfolio Standards are also often reduced to a
yes/no dummy, although real policies differ in targets, timelines, coverage
and flexibility.

rpspanel addresses both problems: one function returns the merged panel with a
codebook and the vintage of every source, and `rps_stringency()` turns
hand-coded, source-cited rules for all 50 states and DC into standardised
annual stringency measures.

### Related software

Several R packages give access to one of the underlying APIs:
[eia](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eia) and
[EIAapi](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=EIAapi) for EIA data,
[bea.R](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bea.R) for BEA data, and
[tidycensus](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=tidycensus) and
[censusapi](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=censusapi) for Census data.
They return each source in its own format. rpspanel differs in that it
harmonises these sources into a single documented state-year panel and adds
RPS stringency measures, which none of them provide. In Python, the
[PUDL](https://catalyst.coop/pudl/) project publishes machine-readable RPS and
clean energy standard data; rpspanel brings comparable policy measures to R
together with the economic and energy variables needed for panel analysis, and
hands the result to [plm](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=plm),
[fixest](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=fixest) and
[csdm](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=csdm) rather than re-implementing
estimators.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

```r
install.packages("rpspanel")
```

or the development version from
[r-universe](https://adebayomoses.r-universe.dev/rpspanel):

```r
install.packages("rpspanel",
  repos = c("https://adebayomoses.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

## API keys

Register for free keys at <https://www.eia.gov/opendata/register.php> and
<https://apps.bea.gov/API/signup/>, then add them to `.Renviron`:

```
EIA_API_KEY=your-eia-key
BEA_API_KEY=your-bea-key
```

## Live example

Everything below is real output, produced by knitting this README against
the live EIA and BEA APIs (`r format(Sys.Date(), "%d %B %Y")`).

### One call builds the whole panel

```{r build, eval = has_keys, message = TRUE}
library(rpspanel)

t0 <- Sys.time()
panel <- build_panel(years = 2001:2022)
Sys.time() - t0

dim(panel)
names(panel)

print(panel[panel$state == "CA" & panel$year >= 2018,
            c("state", "year", "energy_cons_total", "gen_total", "re_share_nonhydro",
              "co2_total", "gdp_real", "population", "rps_nominal")])
```

The first build downloads every series from the seven sources. After
that the data come from the local cache, so the same vintage is used every
time until you pass `refresh = TRUE`.

### Where every number comes from

```{r provenance, eval = has_keys}
attr(panel, "sources")[c("source", "retrieved")]

head(codebook(panel), 8)
```

```{r cite, eval = has_keys}
cite_sources(panel)
```

### A first look at the data

```{r snapshot, eval = has_keys}
snap <- as.data.frame(panel)
snap <- snap[snap$year == 2022 & snap$state %in% c("CA", "TX", "NY", "IA", "WY", "VT"),
             c("state", "co2_pc", "re_share_nonhydro", "gdp_real_pc",
               "elec_price_real", "rps_nominal")]
print(snap, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

National totals match the published figures (2020: about 4,570 million
tonnes of energy-related CO2, 4,010 TWh of net generation, 331.6 million
people):

```{r totals, eval = has_keys}
y20 <- panel[panel$year == 2020, ]
c(co2_mt = sum(y20$co2_total), generation_twh = sum(y20$gen_total) / 1000,
  population_m = sum(y20$population) / 1e6, real_gdp_tn = sum(y20$gdp_real) / 1e6)
```

```{r renewables, eval = has_keys, fig.alt = "Non-hydro renewable share of generation, 2001-2022, states with and without an RPS"}
d <- as.data.frame(panel)
d$group <- ifelse(d$rps_adoption %in% 1, "RPS in force", "No RPS")
avg <- aggregate(re_share_nonhydro ~ year + group, data = d, FUN = mean)

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 2.5, 1), las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = range(avg$year), ylim = c(0, max(avg$re_share_nonhydro) * 1.1),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Non-hydro renewable share", main = "Renewable generation share, state average")
cols <- c("RPS in force" = "#1b7837", "No RPS" = "#8c510a")
for (g in names(cols)) {
  s <- avg[avg$group == g, ]
  lines(s$year, s$re_share_nonhydro, col = cols[g], lwd = 3)
}
legend("topleft", names(cols), col = cols, lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

```{r co2-change, eval = has_keys, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Change in CO2 per capita 2005-2022 against the 2022 nominal RPS requirement"}
w <- merge(d[d$year == 2005, c("state", "co2_pc")],
           d[d$year == 2022, c("state", "co2_pc", "rps_nominal")],
           by = "state", suffixes = c("_2005", "_2022"))
w$change <- 100 * (w$co2_pc_2022 / w$co2_pc_2005 - 1)

par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1), las = 1)
plot(w$rps_nominal, w$change, pch = 19, col = "#2166ac",
     xlab = "Nominal RPS requirement, 2022 (share of sales)",
     ylab = "Change in CO2 per capita, 2005-2022 (%)",
     main = "CO2 per capita change vs RPS stringency")
lab <- w$rps_nominal > 0
text(w$rps_nominal[lab], w$change[lab], w$state[lab], pos = 3, cex = 0.6, col = "grey30")
abline(lm(change ~ rps_nominal, data = w), col = "#b2182b", lwd = 2)
```

### Straight into estimation

```{r fixest, eval = has_keys && requireNamespace("fixest", quietly = TRUE), warning = FALSE}
library(fixest)
feols(log(co2_pc) ~ rps_nominal + log(gdp_real_pc) | state + year,
      data = as_pdata(panel, "fixest"), cluster = ~state)
```

This two-way fixed-effects regression is only an illustration of the
workflow, not a causal estimate.

```{r export, eval = has_keys}
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "us_state_panel.dta")
export_panel(panel, f)      # Stata file + us_state_panel_codebook.csv
file.exists(f)
```

## RPS stringency (works offline)

The RPS measures come from the coding bundled with the package, so they need
no API key:

```{r rps-table}
library(rpspanel)
rps_stringency(c(2010, 2020, 2030), states = c("CA", "WA", "TX"),
               method = c("adoption", "nominal"))
```

```{r rps-plot, fig.alt = "Nominal RPS requirements over time for six states"}
s <- rps_stringency(2000:2035, states = c("CA", "NY", "OR", "IL", "NC", "WA"),
                    method = "nominal")
cols <- c(CA = "#1b9e77", NY = "#d95f02", OR = "#7570b3",
          IL = "#e7298a", NC = "#66a61e", WA = "#e6ab02")

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 2.5, 1), las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(2000, 2035), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "",
     ylab = "Required share of retail sales", main = "Nominal RPS requirements")
for (st in names(cols)) {
  x <- s[s$state == st, ]
  lines(x$year, x$rps_nominal, col = cols[st], lwd = 2.5)
}
legend("topleft", names(cols), col = cols, lwd = 2.5, bty = "n", ncol = 2)
```

Texas shows `NA` here because its standard is set in megawatts. Passing
retail sales (`sales =`), which `build_panel()` does automatically, converts
Texas's and Iowa's targets to a share of covered sales. The conversion assumes
a capacity factor (0.33 by default, adjustable with `capacity_factor =`), so
those values are approximate; they agree with Berkeley Lab's equivalents to
within about one percentage point in every year.

Use `interpolation = "step"` to follow the legal schedule exactly instead of
interpolating between target years. See `vignette("rps-stringency")` for all
five methods.

## Package layers

| Module | Functions |
|---|---|
| Fetch and cache | `fetch_eia()`, `fetch_bea()`, `fetch_census()`, `fetch_rps()`, `rps_cache_*()` |
| Harmonise | `harmonise_states()`, `deflate()`, `convert_units()` |
| Panel builder | `build_panel()` |
| RPS stringency | `rps_rules()`, `rps_stringency()` |
| Documentation | `codebook()`, `cite_sources()` |
| Helpers | `as_pdata()`, `export_panel()` |

## Status of the RPS coding

The RPS rules bundled in `inst/extdata/` code all 50 states and DC: 33
states with a mandatory RPS (including the repealed standards in KS, MT and
WV, and the ended or repealed ones in AZ, OH and TX) and 18 without one. The
RPS rows and the voluntary-goal rows have been checked against the statutes,
DSIRE program pages and the LBNL RPS & CES data (June 2026), and every row
cites its sources in the `source` and `notes` columns (`verified = TRUE` for
all 51). Nebraska is coded as having no RPS: Berkeley Lab counts the
board-adopted clean energy commitments of its public power utilities as a
standard from 2040, but they are utility rather than state policies.
Corrections are very welcome through GitHub issues.

## Data sources

US Energy Information Administration (SEDS, electricity, CO2 emissions), US
Bureau of Economic Analysis (Regional and NIPA accounts) and US Census
Bureau (ACS). The package downloads data on demand and does not redistribute
it.

## Citation

To cite rpspanel in publications, use `citation("rpspanel")`, or cite the
Zenodo record, which always points to the latest version:
<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23480612>.
